questions.prompt: What two components must every correct recursive function have?

options.text: A base case and progress toward that base case

questions.explanation: The base case stops the recursion, and each call must move nearer to it so the base case is eventually reached. Missing either one leads to infinite recursion and a stack overflow.

questions.prompt: What limits the maximum depth of recursion a program can reach?

options.text: The size of the call stack

questions.explanation: Each call pushes a frame onto the call stack, which has a fixed limit. Exceeding it raises a stack overflow, which is why very deep recursion is sometimes rewritten iteratively.

options.text: A call made at the start of the function
A function that calls itself twice
A recursive call that is the last operation in the function

questions.explanation: When the recursive call is the final action, some compilers reuse the current frame instead of adding a new one, so it runs in constant stack space. This optimisation is called tail-call elimination.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea of backtracking?

options.text: Try every complete solution and keep the best
Build a solution incrementally and abandon a partial choice as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer

questions.explanation: Backtracking explores a decision tree, pruning any branch that violates the constraints before going deeper. This pruning is what makes it far better than blindly enumerating all candidates.

questions.prompt: Which classic problem is a textbook example of backtracking?
questions.explanation: N-Queens places queens column by column, abandoning any placement that shares a row or diagonal with an existing queen. Sudoku solving and generating permutations follow the same pattern.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the naive recursive Fibonacci that recomputes overlapping subproblems?
questions.explanation: Each call spawns two more and the same values are recomputed repeatedly, producing an exponential call tree. Memoisation collapses this to O(n) by caching each result once.

questions.prompt: Any recursive algorithm can in principle be rewritten iteratively using:
questions.explanation: Recursion is implemented by the call stack, so simulating it with an explicit stack reproduces the same behaviour without the depth limit of the language runtime.

questions.prompt: How many distinct permutations does a backtracking algorithm generate for n distinct elements?
questions.explanation: There are n choices for the first position, n-1 for the second and so on, giving n! total. This factorial growth is why permutation search is only feasible for small n.

questions.prompt: In backtracking, what does pruning accomplish?

options.text: It cuts off branches that cannot yield a valid solution, reducing the search

questions.explanation: By rejecting a partial assignment the moment it violates a constraint, pruning avoids exploring an entire subtree of doomed candidates. Stronger pruning is what separates a fast solver from a slow one.

questions.prompt: How many subsets does a backtracking algorithm generate for a set of n elements?
questions.explanation: Each element is independently either in or out of a subset, giving 2^n combinations. The recursion branches on include-or-exclude at each element.
